thomas wolf, co-founder of hugging face, joins marina mogilko to discuss the future of open-source ai, the rise of no-code and vibe coding tools, and what job disruption will look like in the next 5 years. they explore who owns ai-generated content, the role of open-source licensing, and how close we are to having robots in our homes. wolf also shares his perspective on whether ai will lead to mass unemployment and how students and professionals can stay ahead. hugging face's 'spaces' feature functions like an app store for ai — users can search, find, and run community-built ai tools (image generation, background removal, text-to-speech) directly in the browser with no coding required. open-source ai models like deepseek can be run locally on your own pc, meaning your prompts never pass through external servers — a key privacy advantage over closed-source alternatives. ownership of ai-generated content is largely governed by the license of the underlying model — most popular licenses (mit, apache) require crediting the original creator but allow commercial use, similar to open-source software conventions. wolf warns that significant job disruption is 'definitely going to happen' within the next 5 years, and advises people studying for long-term careers to factor ai's impact into their planning now. many foundational open-source tools (like numpy or linux) have generated enormous business value for others while their creators earned very little — wolf sees this as a deliberate mission-driven trade-off, with 'open core' as one viable alternative business model. who is thomas wolf app store for ai. what is hugging face who owns what you generate with open-source ai? marina mogilko interviews mit ai lab director daniela rus about the future of work in an ai-driven world. rus explains that people won't lose jobs to ai itself but to colleagues who know how to use ai effectively, and outlines which skills and roles will remain valuable through 2026 and beyond. the conversation also covers edge ai, humanoid robotics, hybrid human-robot teams, and rus's long-term vision for reversing aging. people won't lose jobs to ai — they'll lose jobs to people who know how to use ai more effectively, making continuous ai training essential for anyone in a repetitive or high-volume role. edge ai (running ai directly on-device rather than in the cloud) is already here and is poised to democratize innovation the way the pc did in the 1980s, enabling individuals and small companies to build solutions without costly industrial infrastructure. ai will handle the cognitive aspects of work while robots handle physical tasks, leading to hybrid human-robot teams rather than fully automated 'lights-out' factories in the near term. even in heavily automated domains like customer service chatbots, human presence remains critical for handling unanticipated edge cases that training data doesn't cover. skills tied to curiosity, creativity, strategic thinking, and human interaction are the hardest for machines to replicate and will remain the most durable career assets through at least 2030. intro will ai replace your job? the real threat isn't ai technology that will change everything exclusive: build startups from your phone your morning routine in 2030 robot almost waters $2000 italian shoes live demo: kitchen robot makes lemonade where the money is (nobody's building) robot that fights back (must see) skills that will never be obsolete why memorization still matters her biggest dream: reversing aging daniela, thank you so much for doing this. i'm thrilled to have you on silicon valley girl. wow. thank you so much for having me. i'm excited to have this conversation with you. let's be futuristic straight away. when you think about the future of workforce, do you see any jobs being replaced in the next two or three years by robots or are we still too far from that? a lot of jobs are already enhanced, and in particular the jobs where you have high volume, quite repetitive activity. for instance, chatbots have more or less taken over customer service, but even in the space of chatbots there are aspects that the chatbots cannot handle. i had a recent experience where i was interacting with a chatbot because i had a problem with a shipment and my problem was not captured by the seven options that i could get from the chatbot. i went around and around in circles and then i went to a human at a store and the human said, "well, you have to talk to the chatbot because we don't do that kind of work anymore." my point is that even in these kinds of repetitive scenarios, it is important to have a human presence because there are aspects of tasks that are not anticipated, that are not captured by the data that has been used to train the chatbots. for someone who's doing a repetitive job right now and thinks, well, maybe my job is in line to getting enhanced by a robot or ai, what should they be doing today? they should be training in ai and maybe in robotics. ai will support us with the cognitive aspects of our jobs. robots will support us with the physical aspects of our jobs. in my opinion, people will not lose their jobs to ai, but they will lose their jobs to other people who know how to use ai to be better at their jobs, to be more effective and more efficient. my advice is to keep learning, to stay current, and to understand what is the state-of-the-art with the tools that are most applicable to your domain and to the field you're working in. how do you think robots and ai are going to change the job market?
